case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Medicare Act's reference to hospital patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' includes only patients actively receiving SSI income-supplementing payments at the time of hospitalization, or encompasses a broader category of patients with some SSI connection.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) of the Medicare Act, which governs Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) payment adjustments, cross-referencing Title XVI of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq. (Supplemental Security Income program)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Advocate Christ Medical Center and allied hospital petitioners argue that the statutory phrase 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits' should be interpreted broadly to include a wider range of patients with SSI program connections, including those captured by various SSA payment status codes, thereby increasing the DSH payment fraction and resulting in higher Medicare reimbursements for hospitals serving low-income and vulnerable patient populations. Petitioners contend that the Secretary's narrow interpretation artificially suppresses DSH payments and fails to account for the full scope of patients the statute was designed to cover.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Secretary Becerra and the Department of Justice argue that 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' refers strictly and exclusively to patients who were actually entitled to receive income-supplementing SSI payments during the period they received hospital services. The government contends that petitioners' broader interpretation would improperly include patients who are not eligible for SSI benefits at all, noting that at least 50 of the 74 SSA payment status codes petitioners seek to include are designated 'N' codes indicating ineligibility for SSI payments, and that this narrow reading is supported by case law including Florida Health Sciences Center v. Becerra and Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS.
key_precedents: Florida Health Sciences Center, Inc. v. Becerra, 19-cv-3487-RC, 2021 WL 2823104 (D.D.C. July 7, 2021)
Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 268 (6th Cir. 2013)
Allina Health System v. Sebelius, 982 F. Supp. 2d 1 (D.D.C. 2013)
Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007)
Advocate Christ Medical Center v. Becerra, 80 F.4th 346 (D.C. Cir. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Empire Health Foundation remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I have genuinely wrestled with it across both rounds of deliberation. However, I am persuaded by the structural distinction that Justice Barrett articulates with particular clarity: Empire Health addressed a status-based Medicare Part A entitlement that does not fluctuate month-to-month, whereas SSI's Title XVI architecture makes entitlement inherently month-specific and contingent on ongoing income and resource determinations — importing Empire Health's reasoning wholesale would ignore that 'entitled' carries different operational meaning depending on the statutory scheme it inhabits. Justice Kagan's proposed remand for an eligibility-based standard is administratively creative and not without appeal to my minimalist instincts, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, it would require us to substitute 'meets SSI criteria' for 'entitled to SSI benefits,' which exceeds our interpretive role. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion to myself and write it on the narrowest possible grounds — emphasizing the specific structural differences between SSI and Medicare Part A, declining to foreclose all future eligibility-versus-payment arguments, and leaving open the possibility that Congress or the agency could craft a more nuanced standard through the legislative or rulemaking process.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra remains the most serious challenge to my position, but after careful reflection I find it distinguishable on originalist grounds: Empire Health addressed Medicare Part A, a status-based entitlement program where Congress designed enrollment as a permanent qualifying status, whereas Title XVI's SSI program is architecturally structured as a month-specific cash payment scheme where 'entitlement' is redetermined each month based on income and resources under 42 U.S.C. 1382 — the original public meaning of 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' must be read against Title XVI's own structural design, not imported from a structurally dissimilar program. Justice Jackson's argument that Congress's choice of 'entitled' over 'receiving' suggests something broader than payment receipt is textually interesting, but it proves too much — the original public meaning of 'entitled' in the SSI context, given Title XVI's architecture, is precisely tied to monthly eligibility determinations, and the SSA's 'N' code designations represent affirmative ineligibility findings that cannot be reconciled with any reasonable reading of 'entitled to' benefits. Justice Kagan's proposed remand for an eligibility-based standard is administratively creative but would require this Court to substitute 'meets SSI criteria' for 'entitled to SSI benefits,' which is judicial rewriting rather than interpretation regardless of its policy appeal. The consistent agency interpretation, the structural statutory analysis Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies, and the original public meaning of Title XVI's entitlement framework all confirm that the Respondent's position is correct.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan raises the most serious challenge by invoking Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra, 597 U.S. 423 (2022), arguing that 'entitled' does not require an absolute right to payment but rather satisfaction of eligibility criteria. However, Empire Health addressed Medicare Part A entitlement — a status-based, permanent entitlement arising from age or disability — which is structurally distinct from SSI's month-specific, payment-contingent cash benefit scheme under Title XVI. The critical distinction, as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, is that Congress used 'entitled,' 'eligible,' and 'receiving' with precision throughout the Social Security Act, and Title XVI's own architecture ties entitlement to monthly eligibility determinations — meaning the SSA's 'N' code designation of ineligibility is not a mere administrative artifact but a substantive determination that the patient lacks entitlement in that period. Petitioners' reading would require us to treat patients the SSA itself has affirmatively designated as ineligible as nonetheless 'entitled to' benefits, which is not a strained administrative interpretation but a direct contradiction of the statutory text's plain meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson both press the Empire Health Foundation argument with force, and I want to engage it honestly: Empire Health did hold that 'entitled' does not require an absolute right to payment, and I cannot dismiss that precedent lightly. But the structural distinction between Medicare Part A — a status-based entitlement that vests upon meeting qualifying criteria and does not fluctuate — and SSI's month-specific, income-and-resource-contingent cash payment program under Title XVI is not a formalistic dodge; it reflects how Congress actually designed these programs to operate, and the word 'entitled' necessarily carries different operational meaning in each statutory context. Justice Jackson's point that Congress could have said 'receiving SSI payments' but chose 'entitled' instead is genuinely interesting, but that argument proves too much — Congress also could have said 'eligible for' SSI benefits, as it did elsewhere in the Social Security Act, and its choice of 'entitled' in a cross-reference to Title XVI's architecture, where entitlement is determined monthly, most naturally reads as requiring that monthly entitlement determination to be satisfied. My deepest concern remains the real-world impact on safety-net hospitals and the vulnerable populations they serve, but I cannot in good conscience stretch 'entitled to' SSI benefits to cover patients the SSA itself has affirmatively coded as ineligible — that is a legislative fix, not a judicial one.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Empire Health's reasoning doesn't translate to SSI because SSI is a month-specific cash payment program is the most carefully reasoned challenge to my position, and I acknowledge its force — the structural distinction between a status-based enrollment program and a monthly eligibility determination is real and legally significant. However, I remain unpersuaded that this distinction fully resolves the interpretive question, because the DSH formula's purpose is to measure the low-income patient population served by safety-net hospitals, and the Secretary's reliance on SSA payment codes creates a proxy that may systematically undercount genuinely SSI-eligible patients for reasons unrelated to their substantive eligibility status. The majority's position also fails to adequately grapple with the asymmetry Empire Health identified — 'entitled' was deliberately chosen over 'receiving,' and while the SSI program's monthly structure gives that choice different operational content than in the Medicare Part A context, it does not eliminate the gap between substantive eligibility and actual payment receipt that petitioners identify. I would maintain my position favoring a remand for an eligibility-based standard, while conceding that the 'N' code patients Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor identify as affirmatively ineligible represent a legitimate limiting principle that the agency must address on remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra remains the strongest challenge to my position, and I have genuinely wrestled with it — but the distinction between Medicare Part A's status-based, permanent entitlement and SSI's month-specific, income-and-resource-contingent cash payment program is not a formalistic dodge; it reflects the actual statutory architecture Congress built in Title XVI, where 42 U.S.C. 1382 makes entitlement inherently monthly and contingent. Justice Jackson's argument that Congress could have said 'receiving SSI payments' and chose 'entitled' instead has surface appeal, but the textualist move cuts the other way: Congress cross-referenced Title XVI specifically, and Title XVI's own structure defines entitlement as a monthly determination — so 'entitled to' SSI benefits under Title XVI means what Title XVI says it means, not what a decontextualized reading of 'entitled' might suggest. The SSA's 'N' code designations are not mere administrative artifacts but substantive ineligibility determinations, and accepting petitioners' reading would require me to treat patients the administering agency has affirmatively found ineligible as nonetheless 'entitled' — that is not interpretation but rewriting. My textualist methodology demands that I give effect to Congress's precise word choices in their statutory context, and that context here firmly supports the Respondent's position.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I have genuinely wrestled with it across both rounds of deliberation — but I am ultimately persuaded that the structural distinction between Medicare Part A's status-based entitlement and SSI's month-specific, income-and-resource-contingent cash payment program is legally dispositive, not merely formalistic. Justice Jackson's point that Congress could have said 'receiving SSI payments' but chose 'entitled' instead has some force, yet as Justice Gorsuch correctly observes, the precision argument cuts the other way too: Congress also knew how to say 'eligible for' and chose neither that phrase nor 'receiving,' suggesting 'entitled' carries the specific operational meaning Title XVI's own architecture assigns to it — a monthly determination of payment eligibility. My institutionalist concern reinforces this conclusion: accepting petitioners' reading would require the Court to substitute 'meets SSI criteria' for 'entitled to SSI benefits' in the DSH formula, which is legislative work that Congress, not this Court, should undertake if the current statutory scheme produces undesirable results for safety-net hospitals. The consistent agency interpretation, the structural statutory analysis, and the 'N' code problem Justice Sotomayor identifies all counsel maintaining the Respondent position on the narrowest possible textual grounds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan's Empire Health Foundation argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I have given it careful consideration across both deliberation rounds. However, I am now more confident — not less — that Empire Health does not control here, for the reason Justice Thomas articulates with precision: Medicare Part A entitlement is a status-based right that, once established, does not fluctuate month-to-month, whereas SSI entitlement under Title XVI is structurally month-specific, contingent on ongoing income and resource determinations under 42 U.S.C. 1382. Justice Kagan's proposed remand for an eligibility-based standard is administratively creative, but as I noted in my prior reasoning, it requires substituting 'meets SSI criteria' for 'entitled to SSI benefits' — a rewrite, not an interpretation — and the SSA's 'N' code designations represent affirmative ineligibility determinations that cannot be reconciled with any reasonable reading of 'entitled.' Justice Jackson's point that Congress could have written 'receiving SSI payments' but chose 'entitled' instead is textually interesting, but the better inference from that choice is that Congress tracked SSI's own entitlement architecture, not that it intended a broader eligibility standard the statute's text and structure cannot support.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Empire Health Foundation does not translate to SSI because SSI is a month-specific cash payment program is the most carefully reasoned opposing argument, and I take it seriously — but I remain unpersuaded that the structural distinction between Medicare Part A and SSI is as decisive as my colleagues suggest. The core insight of Empire Health is that 'entitled' in the DSH formula context signals something about eligibility status rather than actual payment receipt, and that interpretive principle does not evaporate simply because SSI's underlying entitlement determinations are made monthly rather than permanently. Justice Gorsuch's precision argument — that Congress used 'entitled,' 'eligible,' and 'receiving' with deliberate distinction — actually supports my position: if Congress wanted to limit the DSH numerator to patients actively receiving SSI checks, it could have written 'receiving' or 'being paid,' but it chose 'entitled to,' which in the context of the DSH formula's structural purpose of measuring low-income patient burden, most naturally reads as satisfying the substantive criteria for SSI. I acknowledge the 'N' code problem Justice Sotomayor raises is real and requires a limiting principle, but that difficulty in line-drawing does not justify adopting the Secretary's payment-receipt standard wholesale when it demonstrably excludes patients who satisfy SSI's substantive eligibility criteria for purely administrative reasons unrelated to their actual poverty status.

John Roberts.reasoning: The statutory text of 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) references patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' and as Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 268 (6th Cir. 2013) correctly recognized, the structural differences between SSI and Medicare Part A are dispositive: SSI benefits are monthly cash payments contingent on ongoing eligibility, not a status-based entitlement like health insurance coverage. The Secretary's interpretation that 'entitled' means actually eligible to receive SSI payments during the hospitalization period is consistent with how Title XVI itself operates — entitlement to SSI is month-specific and can be lost, unlike Medicare Part A entitlement which is permanent and automatic. Petitioners' broader reading would sweep in patients bearing SSA 'N' codes explicitly designating SSI ineligibility, which strains the statutory text beyond any reasonable construction and would effectively rewrite the DSH formula Congress enacted. Consistent with my preference for narrow, textually grounded rulings that respect agency interpretations supported by structural statutory analysis and circuit court precedent, I would affirm the D.C. Circuit's judgment for the Secretary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying strict textualism and the original public meaning of 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' the statutory text most naturally refers to patients who are actually entitled to receive SSI cash payments during the relevant period, not merely those with some attenuated SSI connection. The word 'entitled' in the Social Security Act context has a specific legal meaning denoting actual eligibility for and receipt of benefits, and Congress's use of this precise term in 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) must be given its ordinary legal meaning at the time of enactment. The petitioners' expansive reading would sweep in patients designated under SSA 'N' codes explicitly indicating SSI ineligibility, which directly contradicts the plain statutory text and would effectively rewrite the provision to read 'patients with any SSI connection' rather than patients 'entitled to' benefits. Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS and Florida Health Sciences Center v. Becerra correctly applied the textual meaning, and while I am sympathetic to the hospitals' policy arguments about serving vulnerable populations, it is Congress's prerogative, not the judiciary's, to broaden the DSH formula if it chooses.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text of 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) refers specifically to patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' and as a textualist, I must give these words their precise statutory meaning. Unlike Medicare Part A entitlement, which is automatic and permanent upon qualifying age or disability, SSI benefits are monthly cash payments contingent on an individual's income and resources in a given month — meaning 'entitlement' to SSI is necessarily a month-specific determination, not a status that persists independently of actual payment eligibility. The Sixth Circuit in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248 (6th Cir. 2013), correctly recognized this structural distinction and upheld the Secretary's narrow interpretation, and the petitioners' proposed expansion to include patients designated under 'N' codes — which SSA itself designates as indicating ineligibility for SSI payments — would effectively rewrite the statute to include individuals who are, by the agency's own classification, not entitled to SSI benefits at all. Adopting the petitioners' broader reading would require this Court to ignore the plain meaning of 'entitled' as used in the SSI statutory scheme and substitute a judicially invented category untethered to the statutory text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: While my sympathies lie with hospitals serving vulnerable low-income populations, the statutory text of 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) and the structural differences between SSI and Medicare Part A benefits compel me to side with the Secretary here. As the Sixth Circuit recognized in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248, 268-69 (6th Cir. 2013), SSI benefits are month-specific cash payments, not an ongoing insured status like Medicare Part A, meaning 'entitled to SSI benefits' necessarily refers to active entitlement during the hospitalization period rather than some broader programmatic connection. The petitioners' expansive reading would sweep in patients designated under 'N' codes—patients the SSA itself has determined are ineligible for SSI payments—which strains the statutory language beyond its natural meaning and would effectively rewrite the DSH formula Congress enacted. Though I am deeply concerned about the real-world impact on safety-net hospitals and the low-income patients they serve, the proper remedy for an underfunded DSH system lies with Congress, not with judicial expansion of statutory text beyond what it can reasonably bear.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The statutory phrase 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' is most naturally read by reference to SSI's own eligibility framework under 42 U.S.C. 1382, which distinguishes between categorical eligibility—meeting the income, resource, and disability criteria—and the administrative act of payment. As the Court recognized in Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra, 597 U.S. 423 (2022), 'entitled' in the Medicare DSH context does not require an absolute right to payment but rather satisfaction of program eligibility criteria, and applying that same logic here counsels against the Secretary's hyper-narrow reading that excludes patients who satisfy SSI's substantive criteria but missed a payment for administrative reasons like an invalid mailing address. The Secretary's interpretation, which relies on SSA payment status codes—including 'N' codes that may sweep in genuinely ineligible individuals while excluding genuinely eligible ones—creates exactly the kind of agency-crafted instability that undermines the DSH formula's structural coherence and its purpose of measuring the low-income patient population. A pragmatic reading of the statute that anchors entitlement to SSI eligibility criteria rather than month-to-month payment receipt better serves statutory purpose, administrative workability, and the congressional design of compensating hospitals for the genuine costs of serving vulnerable populations, though I would remand to the agency to craft a workable eligibility-based standard that excludes the clearly ineligible 'N' code patients.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain meaning of 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' most naturally refers to patients who actually hold a legal right to receive SSI monetary payments during the relevant period, not merely those with some administrative connection to the SSI program. Across the Social Security Act's statutory scheme, Congress consistently distinguished between 'entitled,' 'eligible,' and 'receiving' benefits with precision — as evidenced by 42 U.S.C. 1396a(a)(10)(A)(i)(II)'s reference to SSI benefits 'being paid' and 42 U.S.C. 1320b-19(k)(4)'s definition of beneficiary status month-by-month based on eligibility for payments. Petitioners' proposed expansion to include patients assigned 'N' codes — which the SSA itself designates as indicating ineligibility for SSI payments — would stretch the statutory text beyond recognition and effectively rewrite the numerator of the DSH fraction in a manner Congress did not authorize. The Sixth Circuit's reasoning in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, which applied a similarly narrow reading consistent with the statute's text and cross-referencing structure, reinforces that the Secretary's interpretation reflects the most faithful reading of what Congress actually enacted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory text of 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) references patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' and as the Sixth Circuit correctly recognized in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248 (6th Cir. 2013), the structural differences between the SSI and Medicare Part A statutory schemes justify treating 'entitlement' differently in each context — SSI entitlement is month-specific and payment-contingent, not a permanent status like Medicare Part A enrollment. The Secretary's interpretation that this phrase covers only patients actually receiving SSI income-supplementing payments during the hospitalization period is grounded in the architecture of Title XVI itself, where entitlement is tied to monthly eligibility determinations under 42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq., and the petitioners' broader reading would sweep in patients designated under SSA 'N' codes as ineligible for SSI payments, stretching the statutory text beyond its natural meaning. From an institutionalist and textualist standpoint, where Congress knows how to draft broader coverage language — as evidenced by other statutory provisions referencing SSI beneficiaries more expansively — the Court should not rewrite this provision to dramatically expand DSH payments in ways Congress did not clearly authorize, particularly given the major fiscal consequences involved.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying textualist and originalist methodology, the phrase 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' in 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) most naturally refers to patients who hold an active, present entitlement to receive SSI cash payments during the relevant period, not merely those with some attenuated programmatic connection. Title XVI itself, codified at 42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq., structures SSI as a monthly cash payment program, and Congress's use of 'entitled' throughout the Social Security Act consistently denotes a present, operative right to receive a specific benefit rather than a general eligibility status or program affiliation. The D.C. Circuit's reasoning in Advocate Christ Medical Center v. Becerra, 80 F.4th 346 (D.C. Cir. 2023), and the Sixth Circuit's analysis in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 268 (6th Cir. 2013), correctly identified that petitioners' broader reading would sweep in patients bearing SSA payment status codes explicitly designated as indicating SSI ineligibility, which cannot be reconciled with the statutory text's plain requirement of entitlement to benefits. While I acknowledge the petitioners raise a non-frivolous argument that 'entitlement' need not mean actual receipt of payment—as Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra, 597 U.S. 434 (2022), cautioned against equating entitlement with an absolute right to payment—the specific cross-reference to Title XVI's cash-payment structure and the government's consistent administrative interpretation counsel in favor of the Secretary's narrower reading.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The statutory phrase 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' should not be read so narrowly as to exclude patients who meet SSI eligibility criteria simply because they received no cash payment in a given month due to administrative or technical reasons unrelated to their underlying low-income status. As the research materials note, the Supreme Court in Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra, 597 U.S. 434 (2022), rejected equating 'entitled' with an 'absolute right to payment,' and that reasoning applies with equal force here — the DSH formula's population-measuring purpose is best served by capturing the full scope of low-income, vulnerable patients Congress intended to protect, not merely those who cleared every administrative hurdle to receive a cash disbursement in a specific month. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that the Secretary's hyper-narrow interpretation systematically undercounts the most vulnerable patient populations, suppressing DSH payments to safety-net hospitals that serve them and producing practical consequences Congress could not have intended. However, I acknowledge the government's legitimate concern that including 'N' code patients who are affirmatively ineligible for SSI payments would stretch the statute beyond its text, and I would remand for the agency to develop a more principled distinction between those who are eligible-but-unpaid versus those who are genuinely ineligible.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Medicare Act's reference to hospital patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' includes only patients actively receiving SSI income-supplementing payments at the time of hospitalization, or a broader category of patients with some SSI-related status.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) of the Medicare Act, which governs Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) payment adjustments by referencing patients 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI' of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Advocate Christ Medical Center and other hospitals) argue for a broader interpretation of 'entitled to' SSI benefits, contending that the Secretary's narrow reading of the statute improperly excludes patients who hold various SSI payment status codes, thereby artificially deflating DSH payment calculations and resulting in significantly reduced Medicare reimbursements to hospitals that serve large numbers of low-income patients. They assert that up to 74 SSA payment status codes should qualify as indicators of SSI entitlement, which would increase the DSH fraction and corresponding supplemental payments to safety-net hospitals.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra) argues that 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits' refers strictly and narrowly to patients who were actually receiving income-supplementing SSI payments under Title XVI at the time they received hospital services. The Secretary contends that at least 50 of the 74 SSA payment status codes cited by petitioners carry 'N' designations indicating the patient was not eligible for SSI payments, and that including such individuals would improperly expand the DSH fraction beyond its statutory meaning. The Secretary further argues that case law supports this interpretation and that differences in statutory language between the SSI and Medicare schemes justify the apparent inconsistency in how 'entitled' is applied.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett's same-sentence canon argument continues to press hardest against my position, and Justice Jackson's movement to the Petitioner side — grounded in precisely the same reasoning — gives me genuine pause. However, I remain unpersuaded that Empire Health Foundation's interpretive principle about 'entitled to' translates cleanly across both clauses, because that case addressed Medicare Part A's durable insurance status, not a cross-reference to a program where Congress itself defined the benefit as a monthly contingent payment under 42 U.S.C. 1382. The critical point is that when Congress writes 'entitled to supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' it incorporates Title XVI's own statutory definition of what those benefits are — and that definition is structurally different from Medicare Part A's insured status in a way that satisfies Environmental Defense's requirement of contextual evidence for divergent meaning. My minimalist instincts counsel that where the Secretary has maintained a longstanding, consistent interpretation grounded in the actual statutory architecture of the cross-referenced title, and where reversal would require importing SSA payment-status codes Congress never contemplated into the DSH formula, I should not disturb that interpretation on the basis of a canon that the governing precedent itself acknowledges can be rebutted by context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the definition of what the benefit *is* must be distinguished from what it means to be *entitled to* that benefit is the strongest challenge I face, and I acknowledge Empire Health Foundation's interpretive principle carries real weight. However, I remain unpersuaded because when Congress cross-references 'supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' it does not merely invoke the label 'SSI' — it incorporates the statutory architecture of Title XVI itself, where 42 U.S.C. 1382 makes the benefit a monthly determination contingent on that month's income and resources, meaning the referent of 'entitled to' is structurally different in each clause in a way that satisfies Environmental Defense's contextual exception. Justice Kagan argues that Congress knows how to write 'receiving' when it means active receipt, but this cuts both ways — Congress also knows how to define a benefit as a monthly payment contingent on monthly circumstances, and when it cross-references that benefit, it incorporates that contingency into the meaning of 'entitled to.' I acknowledge the tally has shifted to 5-4 and that Justice Jackson's movement reflects the genuine force of the same-sentence canon, but a well-reasoned dissent grounded in the original public meaning of the cross-reference — which incorporates Title XVI's own definitions — is more faithful to textualism than collapsing the structural distinction between a durable insurance status and a monthly payment-contingent determination.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's same-sentence canon argument continues to press hardest against my position, and I acknowledge that Empire Health Foundation's holding that 'entitled to' describes a legal status rather than payment receipt is not easily cabined to Medicare Part A alone. However, I maintain my position because the canon's presumption of uniform meaning is rebutted here not by mere administrative convenience but by the statutory architecture Congress itself built into Title XVI: when Congress cross-references 'supplementary security income benefits under Title XVI,' it necessarily incorporates 42 U.S.C. 1382's definition of that benefit as a monthly cash payment contingent on that month's income and resources, meaning the referent of entitlement is structurally different in each clause — one attaches to a durable insurance status, the other to a monthly payment determination. Justice Barrett argues this conflates the benefit's definition with the meaning of 'entitled to,' but I disagree: the phrase 'entitled to [X]' cannot be divorced from what X is, and when X is by statutory definition a month-specific contingent payment rather than a durable status, a person coded 'N' for non-payment in a given month is not entitled to that payment by the statute's own terms. The tally has shifted and I respect my colleagues' reasoning, but a well-reasoned dissent grounded in Title XVI's own text is preferable to abandoning a structurally sound position simply because five colleagues find the same-sentence canon dispositive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito's structural argument — that Title XVI defines SSI benefits as monthly cash payments under 42 U.S.C. 1382, providing contextual justification for reading 'entitled to' differently than in the Medicare Part A clause — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the reasons Justice Barrett articulates most precisely: the definition of what the benefit *is* does not answer the separate question of what it means to be *entitled to* that benefit, and Empire Health Foundation already established that 'entitled to' describes a legal status of qualifying under eligibility criteria rather than the actual disbursement of funds. The same-sentence canon is particularly powerful here — the Secretary is asking us to read identical language in the same statutory clause to mean 'meets eligibility criteria' for Medicare Part A but 'currently receiving payment' for SSI, and Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp. requires affirmative textual evidence of divergent meaning, not merely structural differences between programs. Justice Jackson's evolution toward the Petitioner position is telling: even a justice deeply attentive to structural program differences recognizes that the Secretary's administrative payment codes bearing 'N' designations are not the kind of clear congressional signal that overcomes the presumption of uniform meaning. From my perspective, the real-world consequence of the Secretary's reading — systematically underfunding safety-net hospitals that serve the most vulnerable patients, including those who are categorically SSI-eligible but temporarily not receiving payment due to month-specific income fluctuations — reinforces that where the text supports the broader reading, we should not strain to adopt the narrower one that harms those the statute was designed to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito's structural argument — that Title XVI's definition of SSI benefits as monthly cash payments contextually informs what 'entitled to' means in the cross-reference — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the reason Justice Barrett articulates most precisely: the definition of the benefit itself is distinct from the legal status of being 'entitled to' that benefit, and Empire Health Foundation already rejected the equation of 'entitled to' with 'actually receiving payment.' The same-sentence canon is not merely a soft presumption here — it is a hard textual constraint that requires the Secretary to produce affirmative evidence of divergent congressional intent, not merely point to structural differences between programs that explain why the mechanics of entitlement differ without explaining why the word 'entitled' should carry categorically different meanings. Justice Roberts's minimalist instinct about not disturbing longstanding administrative interpretations would carry real weight under Chevron, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, Loper Bright has changed the analytical landscape — the question is now purely one of statutory interpretation, and administrative longevity cannot substitute for textual justification. I remain with the Petitioner because the Secretary's reading improperly rewrites 'entitled to' as 'currently receiving,' a substitution Congress demonstrably knows how to make when it intends that meaning.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito's most forceful argument — that Title XVI's definition of SSI benefits as monthly cash payments under 42 U.S.C. 1382 provides the contextual signal rebutting the presumption of uniform meaning — remains unpersuasive to me because it conflates the nature of the benefit with the threshold legal question of whether one is 'entitled to' it. Empire Health Foundation already resolved this distinction: 'entitled to' describes a legal status of qualifying under eligibility criteria, not the act of receiving payment, and that interpretive principle does not evaporate simply because the underlying benefit is structured as a monthly cash payment rather than a durable insurance protection. Justice Barrett correctly frames the burden: the Secretary must demonstrate affirmative textual evidence that Congress intended the same phrase in the same sentence to carry two divergent meanings, and the structural differences between SSI and Medicare Part A — however real — do not constitute the kind of clear textual signal that Environmental Defense v.
